1. // Copyright(c) The Maintainers of Nanvix.

4. // VirtMemoryManager — Specifications (spec phase)
5. //
6. // `VirtMemoryManager` is a zero-sized, stateless singleton façade: every
7. // observable effect lands on the `Vmem` argument(s) (modeled by the inherited
8. // `VmemView` from `mm::virt::vmem`), on returned owned RAII values
9. // (`KernelPage`, `Vec<KernelFrame>`, `Vec<UserFrame>`, a new `Vmem`), or on the
10. // global physical-frame pool (deliberately outside any View). This file
11. // therefore contributes (a) a unit manager View, and (b) the manager-level
12. // vocabulary (pure architectural predicates and range/fork transitions over
13. // `VmemView`) that the manager's `#[verus_spec]` contracts are written against.
14. //
15. // See `view_design.md` for the full rationale.
16. 
17. // Inherited abstractions from the `mm::virt::vmem` module (only available under
18. // `verus_keep_ghost`, which is exactly when this file is included).
19. use crate::mm::virt::vmem::{
20.     is_page_aligned,
21.     page_base,
22.     page_size,
23.     spec_is_physical_region,
24.     spec_is_user_addr,
25.     AddrNat,
26.     PagePerms,
27.     PermView,
28.     UserPageView,
29.     VmemView,
30. };
31. 
32. verus! {
33. 
34. //==================================================================================================
35. // External (opaque) dependency types used only by the manager's contracts
36. //
37. // These types are not modeled by `mm::virt::vmem`'s spec file. They live in
38. // lower-level / sibling crates (the x86 exception error code, the kernel-frame
39. // RAII handle, the ELF file header) and are declared `external_body` so Verus
40. // treats them as opaque. The trust obligation is discharged when those modules
41. // are verified.
42. //==================================================================================================
43. 
44. /// The x86 page-fault error code (`::arch::cpu::excp::ErrorCode`).
45. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
46. #[verifier::external_body]
47. pub struct ExExcpErrorCode(::arch::cpu::excp::ErrorCode);
48. 
49. /// RAII handle for a single kernel frame (`mm::phys::KernelFrame`).
50. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
51. #[verifier::external_body]
52. pub struct ExKernelFrame(KernelFrame);
53. 
54. /// ELF32 file header (`mm::elf::Elf32Fhdr`).
55. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
56. #[verifier::external_body]
57. pub struct ExElf32Fhdr(Elf32Fhdr);
58. 
59. //==================================================================================================
60. // Projection of the opaque page-fault error code into the abstract bit triple
61. //
62. // `is_present` / `is_write` / `is_user` are pure `const fn`s decoding hardware
63. // error-code bits. Their abstract counterparts are uninterpreted projections of
64. // the opaque external `ErrorCode` (a mechanical consequence of that type being
65. // `external_body`).
66. //==================================================================================================
67. 
68. pub trait ErrorCodeBits {
69.     spec fn ec_present(&self) -> bool;
70. 
71.     spec fn ec_write(&self) -> bool;
72. 
73.     spec fn ec_user(&self) -> bool;
74. }
75. 
76. impl ErrorCodeBits for ::arch::cpu::excp::ErrorCode {
77.     uninterp spec fn ec_present(&self) -> bool;
78. 
79.     uninterp spec fn ec_write(&self) -> bool;
80. 
81.     uninterp spec fn ec_user(&self) -> bool;
82. }
83. 
84. //==================================================================================================
85. // Pure architectural predicates (no `&self`, instance-independent)
86. //==================================================================================================
87. 
88. /// A page fault qualifies as a copy-on-write write fault: a user-mode write to a
89. /// present page. Pure decode of the x86 page-fault error-code bits. Whether the
90. /// *page* is actually CoW is read from `vmem@` separately.
91. pub open spec fn spec_is_cow_write_fault(ec: ::arch::cpu::excp::ErrorCode) -> bool {
92.     ec.ec_present() && ec.ec_write() && ec.ec_user()
93. }
94. 
95. /// Membership test for the page run `base, base + PAGE_SIZE, …, base +
96. /// (n-1)*PAGE_SIZE`: `v` is in the run iff it is a page-aligned offset from
97. /// `base` strictly below `base + n*PAGE_SIZE`.
98. pub open spec fn in_page_run(base: nat, n: nat, v: nat) -> bool {
99.     &&& base <= v
100.     &&& v < base + n * page_size()
101.     &&& (v - base) as int % page_size() as int == 0
102. }
103. 
104. /// A mapping is *logically writable* (CoW-eligible at fork time): writable in
105. /// hardware OR already CoW (left read-only with the CoW bit set by an earlier
106. /// fork). Mirrors the docstring of `link_user_pages`.
107. pub open spec fn logically_writable(p: UserPageView) -> bool {
108.     p.perms.write || p.cow
109. }
110. 
111. //==================================================================================================
112. // Range / fork shapes over `VmemView`
113. //==================================================================================================
114. 
115. /// Success shape of `alloc_upages`: exactly the run `[base, base+n*PAGE_SIZE)`
116. /// was added, each page mapped with `perms` and not CoW; everything outside the
117. /// run is bit-for-bit preserved; kernel half and page directory are untouched.
118. /// The backing frame of each new page is an allocator detail and stays
119. /// existential (not pinned here).
120. pub open spec fn maps_user_run_with(
121.     old: VmemView,
122.     new: VmemView,
123.     base: nat,
124.     n: nat,
125.     perms: PagePerms,
126. ) -> bool {
127.     // The user domain grew by exactly the run: a vaddr is mapped afterwards iff
128.     // it was mapped before or it lies in the freshly-allocated run.
129.     &&& forall|v: nat| #[trigger] new.user.contains_key(v)
130.             <==> (old.user.contains_key(v) || in_page_run(base, n, v))
131.     // Pages outside the run are bit-for-bit preserved.
132.     &&& forall|v: nat| #[trigger] old.user.contains_key(v) ==> new.user.contains_key(v)
133.             && new.user[v] == old.user[v]
134.     // Each new page has the requested perms and is private (not CoW).
135.     &&& forall|v: nat| in_page_run(base, n, v) ==> #[trigger] new.user.contains_key(v)
136.             && new.user[v].perms == perms && !new.user[v].cow
137.     // Kernel half and page directory are unchanged.
138.     &&& new.kernel == old.kernel
139.     &&& new.pgdir == old.pgdir
140. }
141. 
142. /// Caller precondition for `link_user_pages`: the child has no user mappings
143. /// overlapping the parent's (relied on by the rollback heuristic).
144. pub open spec fn link_user_pages_pre(parent: VmemView, child: VmemView) -> bool {
145.     forall|v: nat| #[trigger] parent.user.contains_key(v) ==> !child.user.contains_key(v)
146. }
147. 
148. /// Success shape of `link_user_pages` on the `(parent, child)` pair. Every
149. /// present user page of the entry parent is shared into the child at the same
150. /// vaddr and frame; logically-writable pages become CoW in BOTH parent and
151. /// child; genuinely read-only pages are shared read-only (not CoW). The child
152. /// gains exactly the parent's user domain (it had none overlapping on entry —
153. /// see `link_user_pages_pre`). Parent user frames/domain are preserved (only its
154. /// CoW marks may flip); kernel halves and page directories are unchanged.
155. pub open spec fn links_child_cow(
156.     p_old: VmemView,
157.     p_new: VmemView,
158.     c_old: VmemView,
159.     c_new: VmemView,
160. ) -> bool {
161.     // Parent domain & frames preserved; perms unchanged except CoW marking.
162.     &&& p_new.user.dom() == p_old.user.dom()
163.     &&& forall|v: nat| #[trigger] p_old.user.contains_key(v) ==> {
164.             &&& p_new.user.contains_key(v)
165.             &&& p_new.user[v].frame == p_old.user[v].frame
166.             &&& (logically_writable(p_old.user[v]) ==> p_new.user[v].cow)
167.             &&& (!logically_writable(p_old.user[v]) ==> p_new.user[v] == p_old.user[v])
168.         }
169.     // Child gains exactly the parent's user pages: same frames, CoW iff writable.
170.     &&& c_new.user.dom() == c_old.user.dom().union(p_old.user.dom())
171.     &&& forall|v: nat| #[trigger] p_old.user.contains_key(v) ==> {
172.             &&& c_new.user.contains_key(v)
173.             &&& c_new.user[v].frame == p_old.user[v].frame
174.             &&& c_new.user[v].cow == logically_writable(p_old.user[v])
175.         }
176.     // Pre-existing, non-overlapping child pages are preserved.
177.     &&& forall|v: nat| #[trigger] c_old.user.contains_key(v) && !p_old.user.contains_key(v)
178.             ==> c_new.user.contains_key(v) && c_new.user[v] == c_old.user[v]
179.     // Kernel halves and page directories unchanged on both.
180.     &&& p_new.kernel == p_old.kernel
181.     &&& p_new.pgdir == p_old.pgdir
182.     &&& c_new.kernel == c_old.kernel
183.     &&& c_new.pgdir == c_old.pgdir
184. }

187. // VirtMemoryManagerView — unit View of the stateless manager singleton
188. //==================================================================================================
189. 
190. /// Abstract state of the (stateless) virtual-memory manager singleton.
191. ///
192. /// `VirtMemoryManager` is zero-sized: it owns no mappings, no frames, and no
193. /// page tables. All abstract state a caller reasons about lives in the `Vmem`
194. /// argument(s) (`VmemView`) and in the returned owned values. This marker View
195. /// therefore carries no fields — it exists only so the manager satisfies the
196. /// module's View/`inv()` convention.
197. pub struct VirtMemoryManagerView;
198. 
199. impl View for VirtMemoryManager {
200.     type V = VirtMemoryManagerView;
201. 
202.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> VirtMemoryManagerView {
203.         VirtMemoryManagerView
204.     }
205. }
206. 
207. impl VirtMemoryManager {
208.     /// Internal consistency. The manager has no internal exec fields, so there is
209.     /// no implementation-consistency obligation to encode.
210.     pub open spec fn internal_inv(&self) -> bool {
211.         true
212.     }
213. 
214.     /// Top-level invariant. There is no caller-visible manager-level
215.     /// well-formedness; per-`Vmem` well-formedness is asserted on the `Vmem`
216.     /// arguments of each method.
217.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
218.         self.internal_inv()
219.     }
220. }

 Callers: `mm/elf.rs:304` (merge permissions for a page shared by two segments),

 - On `Ok(())`: the already-mapped page at `vaddr` now has permissions `access`.
 - On `Err`: permissions unchanged; caller propagates. (ELF loader relies on this
   to widen permissions on an overlapping page without remapping.)
 - Caller assumes the page is already mapped (it does not allocate).
 
 ### `alloc_kpage(&mut self, clear) -> Result<KernelPage, Error>`
 
 Callers: `mm/kernel_vas.rs:148`, `pm/kcall/mcopy.rs:46` (scratch page).
 
 - On `Ok(kpage)`: a single kernel page is returned; if `clear`, it is zeroed. The
   returned `KernelPage` owns its frame and **frees it on `Drop`** — `mcopy` relies
   on the scratch page being reclaimed when it goes out of scope.
 - On `Err`: no page allocated; caller propagates with `?`.
 
 ### `alloc_kpages(&mut self, clear, count, kframes: &mut Vec<KernelFrame>) -> Result<(), Error>`
 
 Caller: `mm/kstack.rs:95` (kernel stack frames).

   with `capacity >= count` (else `InvalidArgument`).

   `clear`, each is zeroed. The caller then maps them
   (`map(KernelPage::new)`) into a kernel stack.

 ### `load_elf(&mut self, vmem, elf: &Elf32Fhdr) -> Result<(VirtualAddress, PageAligned<VirtualAddress>), Error>`
 
 Caller: `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:575` (exec), on a freshly created `vmem`.
 
 - On `Ok((entry, args_vaddr))`: ELF segments are loaded/mapped into `vmem`;
   `entry` is the program entry point used to forge the user context, and
   `args_vaddr` is a page-aligned address where the caller then allocates a page
   for argv (via `alloc_upages`). Caller assumes both are valid user-space
   addresses for the loaded image.
 - On `Err`: caller abandons the new `vmem` (`?`); partial mappings inside `vmem`
   are acceptable because the whole address space is discarded on failure.
 - Caller doesn't care: segment layout, how `elf32_load` maps each PT_LOAD, or
   where `args_vaddr` is placed relative to segments.
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 From the caller's perspective, `VirtMemoryManager` is a **stateless service
 (singleton façade) for managing user/kernel page mappings inside a `Vmem` address
 space**, drawing physical frames from the global physical-memory pool. Callers use
 it to: create/clone address spaces (`new_vmem`), populate them
 (`load_elf`, `alloc_upages`, `link_user_pages`), change/remove user mappings
 (`ctrl_upage`, `try_unmap_upage`), resolve copy-on-write faults
 (`try_resolve_cow_fault`), and obtain kernel-side pages/frames
 (`alloc_kpage`, `alloc_kpages`).
 
 ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
 
 - **Transactional on failure.** Mapping operations either fully succeed or fully
   roll back: `alloc_upages`, `alloc_kpages`, and `link_user_pages` leave their
   target `Vmem` (and frame refcounts) as if never called when they return `Err`.
 - **`Ok(false)` ≠ error.** For `try_unmap_upage` and `try_resolve_cow_fault`,
   `Ok(false)` denotes a benign "nothing to do / not applicable" outcome that
   callers branch on; only `Err` is a real failure.
 - **Caller-owned scratch buffers** (`uframes`, `kframes`) must be empty with
   sufficient capacity; the manager validates this and never reallocates them.
 - **Frame ownership flows through RAII.** Returned `KernelPage`/`UserFrame` (and
   those dropped during unmap/rollback) release physical frames on `Drop`; callers
   rely on scope-based reclamation, never manual frees.
 - **User-space confinement.** User-page operations validate that addresses lie in
   the user region; out-of-range inputs yield `BadAddress`/`Ok(false)` rather than
   corrupting kernel mappings.
 - **Manager statelessness.** No observable state lives in `VirtMemoryManager`
   itself; every effect is on the passed-in `Vmem` or the global frame pool, so the
   View must model the address space / frame ownership, not the (empty) manager.

 To callers, `VirtMemoryManager` is a **stateless singleton service** that

 out kernel-side pages/frames drawn from the global physical-frame pool. It is
 obtained via `VirtMemoryManager::get_mut()` and threaded as `&mut self`, but
 `struct VirtMemoryManager;` is **zero-sized**: it owns no fields and carries no
 observable state of its own (caller analysis §"Manager statelessness").

 manager View. Every observable effect lands on one of:
 
 1. the **`Vmem` argument(s)** a function receives — modeled by the *inherited*
    `VmemView` already designed and implemented for the `mm::virt::vmem` module;
 2. the **returned owned RAII values** (`KernelPage`, `Vec<KernelFrame>`,
    `Vec<UserFrame>`, the new `Vmem` from `new_vmem`) — modeled by their own
    type-level views; and
 3. the **global physical-frame pool** behind `PhysMemoryManager` — a *global*
    resource, deliberately left **outside** any single View (parallel to the way
    `VmemView` excludes the global CR3 register and global physical memory; see
    Rejected Alternatives).

 re-evaluation of the **inherited `VmemView`** against the manager's callers, and

 substitution test forces this: a field-bearing manager View could only mirror

289.     /// For each present user mapping in `parent`, this function adds a new reference to
290.     /// the underlying physical frame and installs the same mapping in `child` at the same
291.     /// virtual address. A mapping is treated as *logically writable* when it is writable in

339.         // `parent` while borrowing its page tables via `for_each_user_mapping`, so each
340.         // chunk first snapshots up to LINK_CHUNK entries into a stack-resident buffer,
341.         // then performs the share/map/mark steps. This avoids any heap allocation that
342.         // scales with the parent's mapping count (the kernel slab allocator caps at
343.         // 512-byte requests, which a single Vec proportional to the mapping set quickly
344.         // exceeds).

347.         // vaddr and skips entries already linked by a prior chunk. This makes the walk
348.         // robust against the parent's iteration revisiting entries we have already
349.         // processed (e.g. writable entries that are now CoW-marked but still present).

351.             let mut buf: LinkUserMappingBuf = make_uninitialized_array();
352.             let mut count: usize = 0;
353.             parent.for_each_user_mapping(|vaddr, pte: PageTableEntry| {
354.                 if count < LINK_CHUNK && child.try_find_user_pte(vaddr)?.is_none() {

359.                     // copy-on-write too, rather than as a plain read-only mapping that would

361.                     // state is carried alongside so the link step can skip re-marking an

363.                     let parent_cow: bool = pte.is_cow();
364.                     let writable: bool = pte.flags().is_writable() || parent_cow;
